I see this was chaned in #553 - I would like to reopen the discussion about session storage being a secure location for storing session identifiers.

>1) NIST 800-63B 7.1: 
> Secrets used for session binding SHOULD NOT be placed in insecure locations such as HTML5 Local Storage due to the potential exposure of local storage to cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.

I believe *HTML5 Local Storage* here refers to both window.localStorage and window.sessionStorage from the "Web Storage API", since both are prone to XSS

>Also known as Offline Storage, Web Storage....

And where you going to hold your JWT tokens? :)

My argumentation on that topic: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/696#issuecomment-626231907 and it's waiting for ASVS v4.1
And where you going to hold your JWT tokens? :)

If session token handling is done with cookies, then it's no-brainer to not talk about keeping this value in sessionStorage or localStorage.

Now, if session token is sent to API with bearer header (for example), then where you going to keep session token value (or JWT) on the client-side? With this change you need to solve that situation also.

From attacking perspective - IMO stealing session token and then using it yourself is a bit yesterday. I could automate victim browser with some nice XSS "main in the browser" payload and make victim browser just a gateway. Immediate and effective. You can force victim browser to do everything without making requests to some application from your own IP. I recommend to use HttpOnly for session cookies, but on the other hand - you just need to be sure that you don't have an XSS, otherwise you are `<beep>` anyway.

Effective and efficient usage of Content Security Policy together with interceptors at the application layer, does it not allow secure usage of local storage? If the user browser doesn't have the required features for it to work is it not up to the developer to create a fallback implementation to secure the application? 
Being technology restrictive is bad! Awareness seams to better than denying what can be securely achieved. Automating application security checks and this feature in particular, would raise false positives if the above is implemented, how to go around it?

If 3.2.3 is removed, where does that leave 8.2.2, 3.4.x and 3.5.x? 

8.2.2 seems to suggest that session tokens shouldn't be stored in cookies as they are sensitive information, whereas 3.4.x and 3.5.x in absence of 3.2.3 and 8.2.2 would suggest that utilizing localStorage is acceptable. 

> I don't read this as recommendation but as an example, that even droping requirement is better than that.

Ideally the language would be stronger, but it seems that consensus is alluding us here. As a compromise, perhaps leaving the language vague is better than removing it entirely as references with specific recommendations are available at the end of the section. 

NIST 800-63b, the OWASP Cheat Sheet, and Bugcrowd's Vulnerability Rating Taxonomy all discourage local and/or session storage. 

AWS Amplify is an example of an open source library that utilizes local storage for tokens. That community has been struggling with a similar discussion and there are several open issues referencing potential for failed security reviews (for example, 3436 and 3224).

Do you mean remove 3.2.3, 8.2.2, 3.4.x, and 3.5.x? This would create a major gap in ASVS coverage.

If you mean just 3.2.3, then we need to clarify 8.2.2, which brings us back to the same debate. 

If both 3.2.3 and 8.2.2 are removed, then ASVS lacks guidance on the perils of local and session storage and seems to equate them with httpOnly cookies for session token storage, whereas the properties of these mechanisms are quite different. httpOnly cookies, BFFs, and/or Web Workers seem to be the best practices here. 

Removing requirements related to token security also means that any external security researchers utilizing ASVS for communicating their findings will be unable to directly reference the issue of, for example, tokens being stored in localStorage. They will instead need to reference the Cheat Sheet, NIST 800-63b, or Bugcrowd's VRT, which weakens this use-case for ASVS. 

In my opinion, it's better to have a vague requirement that can then be communicated around and explained than to have no requirement to reference.

Rather than moving httpOnly cookies to L2/L3 as has been suggested, a better solution might be creating a "light" or L0.5 version of ASVS that could accommodate practices that are known to be problematic. One of the challenges with moving more demanding requirements to L2/L3 is that the levels of ASVS seem to be split up on two different axis: whether it can be performed externally (without access to the code) and whether it's required for typical or highly sensitive applications. These two are not always mutually agreeable, as in this case.

Wouldn't removing only 3.2.3 leave ASVS ambiguous? 8.2.2 would still conflict with sections 3.4 and 3.5. 

If the ASVS team has concluded that cookies and browser storage are unusable, it seems that sections 3.4 and 3.5 also need to be removed, as they relate to implementations of cookies and browser storage. 

That would leave ASVS's recommendation for session tokens to be:

> 8.2.2: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data or PII.

Which puts ASVS in conflict with NIST 800-63b, and will require adjusting the explanation of how ASVS relates to NIST 800-63b.

Specifically, this section should probably be changed:

> As previously noted, these requirements have been adapted to be a compliant subset of selected NIST 800-63b controls, focused around common threats and commonly exploited authentication weaknesses. Previous verification requirements have been retired, de-duped, or in most cases adapted to be strongly aligned with the intent of mandatory NIST 800-63b requirements.

> 8.2.2: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) **does not contain sensitive data** or PII.

It's okay for us to disagree about recommendations, but the standard needs to at least be consistent for it to be useful.

I agree 100% with needing to remain consistent. But I do not agree with  giving bad advice. There is no good place to store tokens or sensitive data in the browser as previously discussed, regardless of that NIST or  others say.

But these two requirements are very different.

What I tend to recommend in my practice is:

 1. Use a HTTPOnly cookie if you can for tokens, but it really does not matter since XSS can abuse a cookie
 2. Do not store any sensitive data in the browser and instead use cache removal response headers to ensure that sensitive data can be viewed but does not get persisted.

This is how big banking apps and similar operate, it's not a radical suggestion.

**So to advise not storing sensitive data in the browser (and using cache removal response headers) is not the same as actually SUGGESTING that there is a good place to store session tokens in the browser.**

**Storing session tokens in the browser is a necessary evil and there is no good solution. But that does not mean credit card data, banking account data and similar should be persisted in the browser long term. Very different ideas in play here.**

- Jim

I agree 100% with needing to remain consistent. But I do not agree with  giving bad advice. There is no good place to store tokens or sensitive data in the browser as previously discussed, regardless of that NIST or  others say.

But these two requirements are very different.

What I tend to recommend in my practice is:

 1. Use a HTTPOnly cookie if you can for tokens, but it really does not matter since XSS can abuse a cookie
 2. Do not store any sensitive data in the browser and instead use cache removal response headers to ensure that sensitive data can be viewed but does not get persisted.

This is how big banking apps and similar operate, it's not a radical suggestion.

**So to advise not storing sensitive data in the browser (and using cache removal response headers) is not the same as actually SUGGESTING that there is a good place to store session tokens in the browser.**

**Storing session tokens in the browser is a necessary evil and there is no good solution. But that does not mean credit cards data, banking  account data and similar should be persisted in the browser long term. Very different ideas in play here.**

- Jim

The most simple change might be:

> 8.2.2: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain PII or sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.

or

> 8.2.2: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain PII or non-token sensitive data.

This effectively puts all browser storage (local storage, session storage, IndexedDB and cookies) on equal footing and defers to 3.4.x (cookies) and 3.5.x (token-based) for implementation specifics.

The most simple change to meet the most recently stated goals might be:

> 8.2.2: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as HTML5 local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain PII or sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.

This effectively puts all browser storage on equal footing despite their differing characteristics, and defers to 3.4.x and 3.5.x for implementation specifics. 

It does raise the question of why session tokens are permitted when other sensitive data is not, as session tokens will often lead to access to the same data, including PII.  

The other thing to keep in mind is that this change does not meet the previously stated goal of ASVS not providing bad advice. With the removal of 3.2.3 and this change to 8.2.2, ASVS is advocating for localStorage **or** sessionStorage **or** cookies **or** IndexedDB by including the exception and having further guidance in 3.4.x and 3.5.x.
